entry.title: Naming the movement-task function group
entry.summary: One hundred forty-nine of one hundred fifty consecutive movement-task functions received descriptive names, most at high confidence, by combining the project's inventory labels with vtable and caller evidence.
entry.content:
One hundred forty-nine of one hundred fifty consecutive movement-task functions received descriptive names, most at high confidence, by combining the project's inventory labels with vtable and caller evidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each function in a batch of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, which turned out to be almost entirely the pedestrian movement-task code: go-to-point, route following, wandering, formation, crowd, and related task classes.

What was found

Verified The task virtual-table slots have stable meanings across classes: slot one clones, slot three returns the task id constant, slot five makes the task abortable, and slots eighteen through twenty manage subtasks (create first, create next, control).

Verified Movement tasks carry a second thirteen-slot interface table whose slots the inventory labels do not distinguish from primary slots. Its slot seven copies the target point to an out-param, slot eight reads a per-task float with a slot-ten setter, and slot six holds per-class readiness checks. Every batch entry in these slots was assigned to the correct table by comparing table base addresses.

Verified Simple movement tasks run their per-tick update through slot twenty, which calls slots twenty-two and twenty-three to refresh speed and heading; the slot-seventeen process wrapper calls slot twenty first. One code stub is shared by address between a movement task and several UI layout classes through duplicate folding, with unrelated meanings on each side.

Verified Sixteen functions are non-virtual helpers. Caller analysis attributed twelve to a single owning class, mostly subtask factories used only by one task's create-first, create-next, and control methods.

Inferred The secondary slot-eight float behaves like a per-task arrival radius, with tight values for cover movement, loose values for road crossing, and a unit default for tracking, but no direct consumer was observed.

Unknown One area-search predicate matching model category three could not be named because the meaning of that model category is not established.

What was decided or recommended

  • Named one hundred twenty functions at high confidence from slot contracts, verified rewrites, and vtable proof, and twenty-nine at medium from fully read behaviour with project-style wording.
  • Future naming lanes over movement classes should verify the vtable base address for slots six through eight instead of trusting the slot label alone, since primary and secondary slots share numbering.
  • Caller attribution by nearest symbol should be treated as a hint only; two helpers in this batch belonged to unnamed functions immediately after the attributed one.

How to reproduce it

Re-run the lane's evidence gatherer (disassembly plus string, import, and named-callee collection for every batch function), the vtable scan (pointer scan of read-only data validated against runtime type records), and the whole-text caller scan from the lane scratch folder, then compare each function's slot and callers against the contracts above.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first version of the vtable scan found nothing because type descriptors live in writable data rather than read-only data, and because the type-name prefix contains a literal question mark the matching pattern dropped. Both were fixed and the scan then confirmed one hundred thirty-four functions with no mismatches. Two script-native labels on facing helpers look wrong (vector arguments, float results) and were treated as math helpers instead.

entry.title: One table builder verified, and the compiler hides spills inside push sequences
entry.summary: A 1,672-byte input table builder with twelve call sites verified over one thousand trials with zero failures, and the work found a spill pattern other lanes should look for: this compiler stores table pointers into dead argument slots in the middle of pushing another call's arguments, where the writes land above the stack pointer and are easy to miss. Two misread stack offsets each built a self-consistent false theory of wild reads that cost real time; both broke the moment a varying input failed to move the supposedly dependent value.
entry.content:
A 1,672-byte input table builder with twelve call sites verified over one thousand trials with zero failures, and the work found a spill pattern other lanes should look for: this compiler stores table pointers into dead argument slots in the middle of pushing another call's arguments, where the writes land above the stack pointer and are easy to miss. Two misread stack offsets each built a self-consistent false theory of wild reads that cost real time; both broke the moment a varying input failed to move the supposedly dependent value.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring input interface functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the checker, at least one thousand trials each, with one deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

  • Verified The smaller function verified 1000/1000 with zero failures, bit-exact floats, thirteen branch shapes, all eight callees firing, and its wrong version caught. Most trials complete; a minority fault identically on both sides when a record counter nears its cap.
  • Verified While pushing one call's arguments the original stores three table pointers into the dead slots of its own earlier integer arguments, plus a byte offset and a counter into two more. The inner loop then reads tables where a naive read sees dead arguments and uninitialised stack. The stack comparison stays off for this function and every stored value is observed through call arguments or globals instead.
  • Verified Rust integer division by zero raises a different fault code than the original's divide instruction (a language exception versus a divide error), so zero divisors are excluded from the contract and recorded as a narrowing. Quotient overflow is unreachable because the dividends are small differences.
  • Verified The larger function triaged clean: its thread-local read is the standard scriptable pattern, its four indirect calls all plant through fabricated objects, and its trailing call returns into a shared epilogue. No blocker found; it needs a longer session and a retry kit was left.

What was decided or recommended

The smaller function is recorded as verified with its narrowings stated. The larger is untouched for a fresh lane with the retry kit. Recommended for other lanes: compute every stack-relative target by machine arithmetic along each straight-line path before modelling it, and distrust any hand-tracked offset the moment a varying input fails to move the value that should depend on it. Also check push sequences for writes above the stack pointer, not just below it.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the function and emulate the stack pointer forward through each branch-free stretch, printing every stack-relative operand's target relative to the incoming frame. The three spill writes land on argument slots while a call's own arguments sit below. The contract then plants heap objects for the record buffer, cycles the two flag bytes through all three branches, cycles the record counter across its cap and both signedness edges, and keeps divisors non-zero. Pinning the entry register to heap versus null changes nothing, which confirms no entry register is read.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two transcription slips (one hex offset read as decimal, one disp byte misread) each produced a complete, confident, wrong story: wild reads through sums of pointers, branches that could never complete, a filler transport that was never needed. Each story survived several consistency checks because the checks reused the same wrong arithmetic. What finally broke them was cheap and empirical in both cases: pin a heap word and the original ignores it, sweep one input and the output never moves. About half the lane went to those two detours; the fix in each case was a few lines once seen.

entry.title: Retry lesson: re-derive every offset from the addressed bytes, even from a trusted kit
entry.summary: Verified A retry batch of two large deferred functions verified both, but the second lost most of an hour to table offsets copied from the first lane's kit without re-deriving them: flag bytes live 4 and 5 bytes past the row start, not 0x48 and 0x49, and the record qwords 8 and 0x10 past, not 0xC and 0x14. The kit's author had read an address ending 0xE48 as base-plus-0x48 when the base ends 0xE44, so every offset was 0x44 too high, and the retry's "independent" trace parroted the same error.
entry.content:
Verified A retry batch of two large deferred functions verified both, but the second lost most of an hour to table offsets copied from the first lane's kit without re-deriving them: flag bytes live 4 and 5 bytes past the row start, not 0x48 and 0x49, and the record qwords 8 and 0x10 past, not 0xC and 0x14. The kit's author had read an address ending 0xE48 as base-plus-0x48 when the base ends 0xE44, so every offset was 0x44 too high, and the retry's "independent" trace parroted the same error.

What was asked

Finish two functions an earlier production lane deferred for lack of time: a 952-byte message builder with twenty call sites, three virtual calls and a float loop, and a 2320-byte joystick classifier with a 64-step name and identifier chain plus a record-writing tail.

What was found

  • Verified The message builder verified clean: 1000 of 1000 trials, six branch shapes, all 21 callee slots fired, mutant caught through the calls comparison. Its two image constant blocks were varied per trial through read-only-data fills so the single-precision transcription is genuinely exercised rather than evaluated at all-zero constants.
  • Verified The classifier's retry kit contained three errors: the row offsets above, a claim that a register still held a string buffer at the tail when the code reloads it with the record pointer first, and an out-pointer listed as argument zero of a three-argument call when pushing order puts it at argument two. The retry caught the second two by tracing but copied the first, then spent most of an hour proving the execution "impossible" before re-subtracting the addresses.
  • Verified The classifier's unpatched string helpers cannot be called by the rewrite because the checker's anti-cheat revokes code pages under it, so the rewrite reimplements the case-insensitive and counted compares. Both were verified instruction by instruction against the helpers' own code, and case-flipped trial inputs prove the folding matches.
  • Verified A 71-entry trial rotation with a chain simulator asserting every trial hits its intended exit covers all 31 string tests, all 33 identifier members, both inline outcomes and the probe path; rotation length 71 is prime so every shorter script period decorrelates across exits.

What was decided or recommended

Both rewrites were accepted. Retry lanes should treat a previous lane's kit as unverified input and re-derive every address, offset and argument index from the bytes before building on it; a kit that is right about thirty facts still costs an hour when the thirty-first is wrong. The offset error pattern to watch for is a base address whose low digits are nonzero, where the offset must be subtracted, never read off the end of the constant.

How to reproduce it

Run the batch's two proof contracts through the version 6 driver at 1000 trials each and confirm zero failures with caught mutants; confirm the classifier's row layout by subtracting the table base from each addressed constant in its tail; and re-run the trial simulator to confirm all 70 chain trials hit their intended exits with no shadowing.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified With the wrong offsets, the globals comparison showed the same values in a different order on the two sides, which looked like the original was writing different rows or the worker was misreporting. Four debug contracts with split globals ranges narrowed it to one word before the actual cause, a 0x44 subtraction error, was spotted. Separately, an early reading of the relocation table repeated the classic double-added-base mistake and reported nothing relocated; the coordinator's reloc script is the authority.

entry.title: Hourly reviews, 6 October
entry.summary: The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour: whether the work is still pointed at the goal, what the last hour produced, what weakened confidence in the results, and what changes because of it. One row is added here per review. The day before's rows are in the entry "Hourly reviews, 5 October".
entry.content:
The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour: whether the work is still pointed at the goal, what the last hour produced, what weakened confidence in the results, and what changes because of it. One row is added here per review. The day before's rows are in the entry "Hourly reviews, 5 October".

What was asked

To check every hour that the project is going in the right direction and to improve the process from what was just learned.

What was found

TimeMain findingDecision
00:0516,048 functions verified, 42.9% of the functions and 28.6% of the code by size: 219 functions and 56,000 bytes in the hour, the best hour since the morning, with 28 lanes running. By the launcher's clock large-function lanes made 2,370 bytes per lane-hour (48 of 56 verified) and small-function lanes 2,300 (104 of 110). Direction: 141 methods of six class families are lifted with their proof in the pipeline. Trust, three results. First, the emulator question is measured. A probe with no game code ran 269 float instruction sequences on this machine and on the pipeline's real x86 runner: 24 give different result bits and 130 more differ only in status flags. The differences that matter are the float stack's precision setting being ignored for add, subtract, divide and square root, a signalling not-a-number not being quieted on a 64-bit load, the sign of the result of a masked invalid operation, and the low bits of sine, cosine and arctangent. Counted from the game's code, 85 of 38,381 game functions use those instructions and 3 of the verified ones do: the game computes in the vector instruction set and uses the float stack almost only to return values. Two of the probe's own expectations turned out wrong on real hardware (an 80-bit load does not quiet a signalling not-a-number, and a vector minimum raises the invalid flag for a quiet one), which is what running it there was for. Second, the last strengthening lane re-proved all 47 of its blind proofs and found two rewrites wrong in ways unrelated to signedness: one returned early where the original runs a second block, and one stored the wrong constant into a structure on its stack, hidden because the proof skipped the pointer to that structure and compared nothing in its place. Third, a count from the contracts: 2,992 verified functions skip an argument without observing what it points to.The probe is in the workspace and runs in the pipeline on every push; its results from real hardware are kept beside the emulator's. The 85 functions that use emulator-sensitive instructions are listed, and their proofs are to be repeated on a real x86 machine, which needs the owner's hardware. An audit lane is adding snapshots to a sample of 60 proofs that skip a pointer and counting how many tracked rewrites then fail. Coordinator commits now hold a lock the tick honours, after a tick's commit took a staged crate into a routine commit. Stop doing: treating a lane's reading of documentation as the reference when the real thing can be run; two of thirty-six expectations were wrong. The kernel pool is at 17.5 GB.

entry.title: A signed bound check and a silent contract hole in one batch
entry.summary: Twenty-six small table-manager routines were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent, and the batch surfaced two things worth knowing: one routine bounds its table index with a signed compare that admits very large index values, and the contract linter does not check global address ranges, so wrong ones pass silently with reduced coverage.
entry.content:
Twenty-six small table-manager routines were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent, and the batch surfaced two things worth knowing: one routine bounds its table index with a signed compare that admits very large index values, and the contract linter does not check global address ranges, so wrong ones pass silently with reduced coverage.

What was asked

Rewrite thirty small neighbouring routines from the files-memory area and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the checker, one contract per routine, each with its own deliberately wrong version.

What was found

Verified The batch is one subsystem: two handle tables with an init, register and reset routine each, a pool table with init and find-and-mark routines, a chunk table, an object table teardown, four tick-to-float converters sharing one query helper, three fixed-field name setters, a mode dispatcher with its cache and readiness gates, two access predicates, and a few open, snapshot, shutdown and scan helpers.

Verified The handle-register routine checks its index with a signed 16-bit upper bound after a signed full-word sign check. Small and negative full-word values are rejected, but an index whose low half sits in the top half of the 16-bit range passes and addresses memory before the table, down to 256 KB below it for the largest admitted value. The rewrite keeps the behaviour and the proof covers those values; live callers presumably never pass them.

Verified One scanner routine reads its object base from entry registers whose saved slots overlap a temporary, so its behaviour depends on caller registers the checker cannot transport to a rewrite; it was deferred, not guessed at.

Verified One drain loop exits only when its callees clear a global flag, which intercepted callees cannot do, so any trial entering the loop would run to the call cap; it was deferred with the analysis recorded.

What was decided or recommended

Twenty-six routines count as verified, each over one thousand trials with branch coverage confirmed from the verdicts and a caught wrong version. The lint and schema checks should plausibility-check global address ranges: six contracts in this lane used ranges with a dropped digit, still passed, and were caught only because verdict branch shapes showed paths never taken. Seeding read-only globals is silently ignored and should either work or warn.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the stock checker driver and worker; every verdict records full branch shapes and a failing wrong version. The signed-bound behaviour can be re-derived by reading the index compare and the sign-extending move that follows it in the register routine. The silent-range behaviour is preserved in the lane's early probe verdicts, where two misdeclared ranges passed all comparisons.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two rewrites first failed on missed register reloads just before a return, one branch was read inverted, one multi-argument call passed its words in push order instead of argument order, and code-pointer constants had to be relocated exactly as the original's loader fixups do. Each was caught by the first probe run and fixed from the checker's first mismatch. A build file lock from a lingering scan was worked around by moving the old library aside.

entry.title: The optimizer can delete the reads a fault-parity proof needs
entry.summary: Verified A logically identical Rust rewrite of a filter-matching predicate survived memory reads the original faults on, because the compiler proved the result from the arguments alone and skipped the reads. Marking the reads volatile restored fault parity with no change in logic.
entry.content:
Verified A logically identical Rust rewrite of a filter-matching predicate survived memory reads the original faults on, because the compiler proved the result from the arguments alone and skipped the reads. Marking the reads volatile restored fault parity with no change in logic.

What was asked

Rewrite sixteen small motion-tree routines in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the project checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, written memory, outgoing calls and faults over one thousand trials each.

What was found

Verified One predicate reads its entry count from the same table it then walks, so a count of two or more re-reads the count word as an entry pointer and faults. The first rewrite transcribed the loop faithfully, yet on three trials in sixty the original faulted while the rewrite returned normally.

Verified Disassembly of the compiled rewrite showed the cause: the compiler had split the loop into several versions keyed on the argument values, and the version for arguments whose answer is always zero returned without reading a single entry. The reads were logically redundant, so removing them was a valid optimisation of the value computed, but it changed which addresses fault.

Verified Reading the entry bytes with volatile loads keeps every read in program order while still compiling to plain byte loads. After that change the rewrite passed one thousand trials with matching faults on the count-overlap trials, and a deliberately wrong version with an inverted gate failed as required.

Inferred A sibling predicate verified by an earlier lane passed with plain reads only because it takes no arguments for the compiler to split on. Any search loop whose result is fully determined by loop-invariant arguments can fall into this trap.

What was decided or recommended

  • When a pure loop shows original-faults while rewrite-returns, suspect versioned loops before suspecting the logic, and confirm by disassembling the rewrite.
  • Use volatile loads for the fault-relevant reads in such loops, with a comment saying why, rather than restructuring the logic.
  • Keep fault-parity trials (counts that re-read as pointers, short tables) in every such contract: without them the elided reads are invisible.

How to reproduce it

Build a rewrite of an entry-walking predicate whose match conditions depend only on the arguments, include trials where the count word is re-read as a pointer, and run the checker: the correct rewrite fails with the original faulting and the rewrite returning. Disassembling the rewrite shows an early-return path that reads nothing. Switching the entry-byte reads to volatile loads makes the same contract pass.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first failure looked like a logic error in the match conditions, and the conditions were rechecked twice before the compiled code was examined. The mismatch detail only said one side faulted and the other did not, which pointed at the reads rather than the branches once the faulting address (the small count value) was noticed.

entry.title: Naming the event handler and its neighbours
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions covering inverse kinematics, damage events, the ped event handler and movement tasks are now named, with the event virtual table slot map confirmed and extended along the way.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions covering inverse kinematics, damage events, the ped event handler and movement tasks are now named, with the event virtual table slot map confirmed and extended along the way.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of one hundred and fifty unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and grading each name high, medium or low confidence.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into five groups: IK solvers and managers, damage and death events with a killed-suspect orchestrator, about fifty event handler response slots, the event-group update, and movement-task constructors, destructors and clones.

Verified Joining an earlier lane's event method names to the class-analysis vtable slots pins the shared event slot meanings: type, priority, clone, update, affects-ped, subject ped and entity, supersedes, audible range, validity, takes-priority-over and clone-task. Three more slots were identified from code shape: a subject-presence test and a priority flag getter with its clearer.

Verified Each event handler slot builds a specific response task, so the constructor it calls names it: fire threats build walk-round-fire, shocking events pick one of four shocking responses, revival builds revive, and so on. Slots that only clear or forward the pending task were named for that behaviour instead.

Verified Twenty-one consecutive eight-byte functions are one pattern: secondary-vtable deleting-destructor thunks that shift the object pointer and jump to the real deleting destructor. Movement-task constructors and destructors identify their class by the vtable constants they install.

Verified Both IK manager updates first ask the windowing layer whether the game window is minimized, then step. A small entity-kind field read as bits six to nine distinguishes vehicles from peds in the subject getters.

Inferred A routine that merged symbols label as a script-native message sender is called in the memory-free position by two deleting destructors, so the label looks wrong and the routine frees memory.

What was decided or recommended

One hundred and forty-three functions were named, about two thirds at high confidence, following the established per-area conventions. Seven were left empty at low confidence: four kind-dispatched getters whose returned fields are unknown, one virtual-only IK setup helper, and two handler slots whose response-task classes have no recorded vtable. The next naming lane should identify entity-kind value six and the three unknown simple-task vtables near the jump-task family first.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped executable image and decode one known function end to end before trusting the mapping. Gather per-function evidence first: direct callees resolved through the merged symbols, names from earlier lanes and verified rewrites, string references, vtable cross-references, and a caller scan over the code section. Resolve constructor and destructor classes through the vtable constants they install, and event slots through the response-task constructors they call.

What was confusing or went wrong

Early evidence output truncated callee lists to six entries, which hid response-task constructors and made several handler slots look task-free; printing full lists fixed a wrong theory about assessment-only slots. A few production-lane callee names turned out to be weak guesses that contradicted the code shape and had to be ignored. Two functions the inventory lists with size zero are real and were named from their code.

entry.title: Two contract traps that silently unprove a rewrite
entry.summary: A production lane verifying file-handling functions found two ways a passing verdict can cover less than it claims: fault trials compare almost nothing, and aligned input periods silently drop whole branches. Both were caught by reading the verdict, not by a failure.
entry.content:
A production lane verifying file-handling functions found two ways a passing verdict can cover less than it claims: fault trials compare almost nothing, and aligned input periods silently drop whole branches. Both were caught by reading the verdict, not by a failure.

What was asked

Rewrite four medium and large file-management functions in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with the differential checker, with contracts that steer every path and a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified On a trial where both sides fault, only termination and no-cheat are compared. A trial on which the original made two calls and the rewrite made three passed, because both sides faulted later at the same unmapped call target. The fault parity masked a genuine branch inversion in the rewrite, which only surfaced after the fabrication bug behind the faults was fixed. Fault-heavy passes therefore prove termination and little else.

Verified When every pinned input list shares one period with a scripted answer, whole input combinations never occur: three-iteration loops, helper-with-flag combinations and the empty-list wrap path never ran in 1,200 trials. Re-mixing pin periods to values coprime with the script periods took the verdict from four branch shapes to nine with no other change. The branch list in the verdict is the check; pass or fail alone does not show it.

Verified A uniform heap fill can hide a mutant: a trial that skips a shift over all-zero memory passes under a wrong version that skips the same shift, because the skipped writes would have stored identical values. The same inputs with random fills fail as expected.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep fault trials a small minority and treat them as termination-only evidence; a pass driven by fault parity is not a behaviour proof.
  • Give pinned input lists and scripted answers coprime periods, and read the verdict's branch-shape list before filing a function as verified.
  • When a mutant fails thinly, explain the passing trials (fill luck, period alignment) rather than assuming the contract is strong.

How to reproduce it

Run any multi-callee contract with a broken call target so most trials fault on both sides: the verdict passes with only two checks recorded. For the period trap, pin two counts to lists of the same length as an answer script and compare the branch-shape count before and after changing one list length by one.

What was confusing or went wrong

The fault-masked trial looked fully green and was only questioned because the call sequences printed in a debug run differed. The period alignment was only noticed when the branch list showed four shapes where the analysis predicted nine. Both times the verdict file held the answer; the one-line summary did not.

entry.title: Naming a run of scenario, audio, cover and IK functions
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be six small worlds: ambient scenario tasks, a scrollbar display loader, a blendshape pool, audio voice banks, a cover-search pool, and inverse kinematics. All but fourteen are now named, and the run pinned down what several shared task virtual slots do.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be six small worlds: ambient scenario tasks, a scrollbar display loader, a blendshape pool, audio voice banks, a cover-search pool, and inverse kinematics. All but fourteen are now named, and the run pinned down what several shared task virtual slots do.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence for every name and no name where the behavior is unclear.

What was found

Verified The task virtual slots repeat across every scenario class: one slot aborts the subtask and cleans up speech, voice handles and car doors, one returns an interaction distance, and one builds a single subtask from the pool. Matching slots across classes confirmed each meaning.

Verified Four inventory entries are not real function boundaries: one range overlaps the entries after it, and three start in the middle of a neighboring routine. One zero-size entry is a real function of about 260 bytes. Gap routines between entries had to be read to name jump targets.

Verified A merged symbol in the encrypted part of the executable is mislabelled as a script native; it sits in operator-delete positions in destructor after destructor. Names for callees in that region should not be trusted.

Inferred The middle of the run is audio voice-bank code, not ped tasks as clustered: banked entry lists, scene reset on level load, and per-frame updates. The cover-search pool beside it is genuinely task code, but some of its callers carry audio names, so one side's names are wrong.

Unknown Several task type ids checked by the scenario code have no class mapping yet, which caps those names at behavior level.

What was decided or recommended

  • Named 136 of 150 functions: 22 high, 114 medium, 14 empty with low confidence. Pure jump forwarders and mid-function labels were left empty rather than given duplicate names.
  • Recommended: derive the full scenario vtable from reloc evidence, audit merged symbols in the encrypted region, fix the overlapping inventory entries at the source, and settle the audio-versus-task caller names before the cover region is rewritten.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address, and decode one known function end to end first. Gather per-function evidence into one table (calls resolved against merged and verified names, string and import references, caller scan), read the short functions fully, and cross-check vtable slots against the inventory's reloc evidence and already-named methods.

What was confusing or went wrong

The caller scan initially suggested the cover-search pool was audio code, because several callers carry confident audio names; the verified behavior docs for the callees pointed the other way. The lesson held for the whole lane: caller names are hints, and slot shape plus string evidence outranks them.

entry.title: Lift: six pedestrian task classes pick their next subtask
entry.summary: 5 October 2026 — lane l-cls9 (Verified: differential proofs on the 32-bit target; Inferred: slot meanings across sibling classes)
entry.content:
5 October 2026 — lane l-cls9 (Verified: differential proofs on the 32-bit target; Inferred: slot meanings across sibling classes)

What was asked: lift the verified 32-bit rewrites of six pedestrian task classes — seeking cover, fleeing from and walking towards a shocking event, a hit response, ducking, shaking a fist — into portable Rust that owns its data.

What was found: the family shares one shape. Every complex task carries a subtask word and a marks word (bit 0 gates a state check, bit 1 records a pass); clones allocate through a shared manager global and build from member words; and the shocking-event pair shares a liveness gate (set flag plus set mode fires at once, mixed pairs never fire, otherwise the squared position length must exceed a threshold global, computed in a fixed float order). Per-class data and every slot meaning are tabulated in the lane report with the rewrite behind each row.

What was decided: 12 methods across 5 classes are lifted and proven, each against its verified rewrite on the same generated inputs — return value, full object blobs, every call in order with its arguments, floats bit for bit — with a deliberately wrong lift caught alongside. Destructors go to Drop. The rest is recorded missing with reasons: the six heavy cover-seeking methods, two large task builders, thin constructor shells, and one clone whose trailing store into an opaquely built object has no clean lift shape. No method touches the operating system, so nothing needs the platform traits yet.

Two traps for the next lane. A test file named *update* produces a binary Windows treats as an installer, so the test fails to launch with an elevation error; the proof was renamed to tick. And a crashed 32-bit test binary stayed locked against the linker with no owning process visible, so the suite finished in a second build folder under the lane directory. Both are environment quirks, not proof failures.

entry.title: AL stubs leave the log pointer in EAX (lane a-Q12)
entry.summary: 5 October 2026
entry.content:
5 October 2026

Asked: why did a rewrite returning an AL callee's answer as al as u32 mismatch the original's EAX, when the call sequences matched? (Verified: worker source plus a failing then passing proof.)

Found: the worker's al stub answers with scratch in the upper bytes: it masks EAX down to the low byte and ORs in the script byte, but EAX no longer holds the entry value at that point — the logging prologue has overwritten it with the call-log entry pointer. So the observed EAX is (log_base + call_index * entry_size) & ~0xFF | answer_byte. The log index resets to zero for each side, so both sides produce the identical word for identical call sequences. A rewrite must capture the full u32 answer from the callee macro and thread it to the return; truncating to the low byte fails.

Decided: in functions whose return value is threaded through an AL callee, keep ret: eax and return the macro's full word. The comparison is meaningful: it checks EAX threading (which call's answer survives), and a wrong threading or a truncated return fails. Do not switch to ret: al to dodge the scratch bytes — that weakens the comparison.

Reproduce: any contract with an al callee whose answer reaches EAX; the original's EAX reads as a 0x3101xxxx word (the log region).

entry.title: Stale-flags branch and script phase-lock on a staged large function
entry.summary: 5 October 2026 — lane a-Q14 (Verified: checker runs on the stock worker).
entry.content:
5 October 2026 — lane a-Q14 (Verified: checker runs on the stock worker).

Asked: finish the deferred second counted loop of a large staged function from the prior lane's retry kit.

Found, first: the kit's three inferences about the loop were all wrong, and the disassembly was unambiguous. The path-selecting conditional jump sits several loads after a test of a table answer's low byte, with a row word loaded into the tested register in between; since none of the loads touch flags, the branch tests the table answer, not the word it appears to test (compiler scheduling across a long load chain). The short-call site's second argument is the loop counter, not a surviving flags push, and nothing feeds back into the counter. The full-function proof (1000/1000 plus NaN torture, mutant caught) confirms this reading. Lesson: re-derive retry-kit inferences from the instruction stream before building on them.

Found, second: per-trial script cycles can phase-lock so a callee never fires. A length-14 flags cycle with the stack-cycle position offset put every loop-2 trial on even trials, locking a length-2 gate script to one answer; fixing that locked a length-6 word script against the flags cycle instead. Lengths 14/5/7/3 with a quick simulation of which (path, count) combos occur in 1000 trials fixed it. Lesson: simulate cycle interactions before the first probe when a loop's trip condition depends on a cycled input.

entry.title: Naming batch 116: bound stores, zone volumes and scenario tasks
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be seven clean groups: two parallel streaming stores for collision bounds and physics, a quantized zone-volume system, animated-building virtuals, a module cache with version checking, and the ambient-scenario task family. 147 functions were named, 35 at high confidence.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be seven clean groups: two parallel streaming stores for collision bounds and physics, a quantized zone-volume system, animated-building virtuals, a module cache with version checking, and the ambient-scenario task family. 147 functions were named, 35 at high confidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name.

What was found

Verified The first two groups are twin streaming stores for static collision bounds and physics data, registered under their own names with capacities of 500 and 330 entries. Their find, create, release, save and shutdown routines mirror each other instruction for instruction apart from the globals they touch.

Verified Task virtual slot identities were pinned by cross-checking two independent sources: clone, subtask update, first-subtask and next-subtask creation slots all agreed, and a vtable scan proved one hint-less function was the get-in-car scenario's first-subtask builder.

Verified The scenario trigger checks, greeting speech, trapped-in-car barks and phone-call stepper were identified from the literal speech and config strings they reference.

Inferred A nine-function group manages quantized zone volumes: appending them, decoding them to boxes, testing points against them and relinking moved objects. The mechanism is clear but what the zone flags mean in game terms is unknown.

What was decided or recommended

Three functions were left unnamed: one whose far path jumps into the encrypted code range, one dictionary virtual with no callers and no discernible purpose, and one child-release helper built around an unidentified pool routine. Two existing lane names for shared helper routines were found to be wrong and were noted, not renamed. The next naming lane over store code should diff the twin implementations rather than reading both.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function with capstone over bytes fetched by relative virtual address, read referenced strings the same way, scan the read-only data section for vtable pointers into the batch, and scan the code section for direct call sites to establish callers.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first evidence script indexed the memory-mapped image by file offset instead of by relative virtual address, which silently produced plausible-looking but entirely misattributed strings for every data-section reference. All string evidence had to be re-read with the correct accessor, and the experience is worth a check in any lane tooling that mixes the two.

entry.title: Naming batch: base-class vtables name the overrides for free
entry.summary: One hundred forty-three of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and five of the remaining seven turned out not to be functions at all.
entry.content:
One hundred forty-three of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and five of the remaining seven turned out not to be functions at all.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name and no guessing.

What was found

Verified The batch covers cutscene-object methods, streaming slot machinery, animation tables and pools, a small D3D9 loader, vehicle and boat definition tables, ped-type helpers, and ped and MLO model-info methods.

Verified A base class and its subclasses share most vtable slots, so an override inherits its base slot's name. This named eight model-info overrides with high confidence, each confirmed by a call or tail-call to the shared base implementation.

Verified Five queue entries are not functions: four are short tail fragments reached by jumps from the preceding function, and one is jump-table data. Each was checked independently: no callers, no vtable references, padding plus a fresh function after, and the owning neighbour identified.

Inferred Several neighbour names in the same region look wrong: task-flavoured names on routines that operate on model-info objects, script-native guesses inside the encrypted first megabyte, and narrow names on broad init and frame-update functions.

What was decided or recommended

Naming lanes should check gapfill entries for the fragment pattern before naming them, distrust inventory sizes and subsystem tags, and use base-class vtable slots to name overrides. The queue should replace the five non-function entries with the real functions that follow them.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table for the whole batch first: disassemble each function through the mapped image, resolve call targets and callers against the merged name sources, and join vtable slots from the RTTI dump. Read the short functions fully and dump the unclear ones individually.

What was confusing or went wrong

A helper script named after a standard library module silently broke its own disassembler import and had to be renamed. Inventory sizes were wrong on seven entries, so evidence past the true end of a function had to be excluded by hand. One call-site dump repeatedly returned empty output for no clear reason and was abandoned.

entry.title: Seven verified rewrites compared a call's answer the wrong way, and how the last two were found
entry.summary: By the end of 5 October seven verified rewrites outside the leaderboard family had been withdrawn for one and the same mistake. This entry puts the day's findings in one place: what the mistake is, how often it occurs, how it was found from two directions, and what "verified" is worth in the light of it.
entry.content:
By the end of 5 October seven verified rewrites outside the leaderboard family had been withdrawn for one and the same mistake. This entry puts the day's findings in one place: what the mistake is, how often it occurs, how it was found from two directions, and what "verified" is worth in the light of it.

The mistake

The original calls something, compares the value that comes back, and branches with a signed conditional jump. The rewrite holds the returned value in an unsigned word, because that is what the checker's call macros and a plain function pointer give it, and compares it with an ordering operator. In Rust that comparison is unsigned. The two agree for every answer below two to the thirty-first and disagree for every answer with the high bit set. Contracts script a callee's answers by hand, and by hand people script small numbers.

MeasureValueStatus
Verified rewrites that compare a callee's answer with an ordering operator, found from the rewrites' text241Verified (audit lane's scan; a lower bound by design)
Of those measured, proofs that pass with the comparison's signedness flipped52 of 117Verified (two lanes, each function's own contract on the stock checker)
Of those measured, proofs that pass with the bound moved by one56 of 146Verified
Blind proofs read against the originalAbout 75; five rewrites wrongVerified; each wrong one read again by the coordinator before withdrawal
Verified functions whose original compares a call's returned value and follows it with a signed jump, found from the original's code570Verified (coordinator's sweep over every verified function)
Of those, flagged by a coarse count of signed comparisons in the rewriteSeven; two wrong, three right, two needing a closer readingVerified by reading
How good the coarse count isRun on the five rewrites withdrawn earlier, as they were, it catches fourVerified
Proofs made under older checker versions that the current one accepts unchanged178 of 180, none vacuousVerified (separate audit the same day)

Two directions

The audit started from the rewrites: find comparisons whose operand came from a call macro, build the wrong versions, run them through the existing contract. That measures the proofs, and it is how blindness was shown to be common. But its population is defined by what a text scan recognises, and it said so: calls made through a function pointer taken from an object's table are not call macros.

The sweep starts from the original: disassemble every verified function, and after each call look a few instructions ahead for a compare on the returned register, or a register it was copied to, followed by a signed jump, set or conditional move. That needs no checker run and takes thirteen seconds for the whole verified tree. Its population does not depend on how the rewrite spells a call. The two rewrites it found make virtual calls; neither was among the 241.

What this says about the count

  • The mistake is real and rare: seven found among roughly 15,800 verified functions, in a population of a few hundred functions where it can occur at all. The estimate will firm up when a lane has read all 570 sites exactly; the coarse count is known to miss cases.
  • A blind proof is usually a weak proof of a right rewrite: about nine in ten of the blind ones read so far were right. But "usually" is what the checker exists to replace.
  • The age of a proof is not the problem. Proofs made under the first four checker versions pass the sixth unchanged. The problem is a kind of input the method leaves to the lane's imagination: what a callee answers.
  • Every withdrawn rewrite returns only with a contract that scripts the boundary, its neighbours and values with the high bit set, and with a wrong version that is exactly this mistake and must fail. The production brief has required that for new work since the first case.

Decisions

  • All seven are withdrawn; strengthening lanes have repaired and re-proven the first and are working on the rest.
  • A lane is reading all 570 signed sites against their rewrites, site by site, and reporting every disagreement with the earlier hand adjudications.
  • The population at risk is defined from the original's code from now on, not from the rewrites' text.

How it ended (added at 23:00 the same day)

The lane read all 627 signed sites in the 570 functions against their rewrites: 622 right, four different, one an artefact of a function boundary in the inventory. Its verdicts agree with every earlier hand adjudication by four other lanes. Two of the four were new and were withdrawn, which brought the withdrawals for this pattern to nine.

One of the nine was withdrawn in error and has been restored. Its comparison is written unsigned where the original is signed, as the coordinator read it, but for every answer with the high bit set both branches of the original arrive at the same block: the repair lane ran a signed and an unsigned version against the original on 1,200 mixed trials and 600 more with every answer high-bit, and they agree, while a version with the bound moved by one fails. The coordinator had read the comparison and not followed the branches. So the count is eight observably wrong rewrites, not nine; this corrects the heading above and the two changelog entries that say seven and nine.

Six of the eight are repaired, re-proven with contracts that script boundary and high-bit answers and a wrong version with the flipped comparison that fails, and back in the verified tree. Two are still with a strengthening lane.

A limit found the same evening: the checker runs under an emulator

The development machine is an ARM laptop, and the original game is 32-bit x86, so every proof in this project runs the original and the rewrite under the operating system's x86 emulator. The pipeline's runners are real x86 machines. A differential test of a lifted function passed on the laptop and failed in the pipeline on one input: a signalling not-a-number handed back as a 64-bit value on the float stack. A real processor quiets it on the load; the emulator did not. Verified: one case, reproduced on every pipeline run until the test was changed to treat two not-a-numbers as equal, which is what the lift method says.

What follows from it is Inferred, not measured: where the emulator's float stack differs from a real processor's, a proof made here says that the rewrite matches the original as the emulator runs it. Both sides run under the same emulator, so most differences cancel; one that would not is a rewrite that moves a value through the float stack where the original moves it through integer registers, or the reverse. Nothing is known to be wrong because of this. It is the largest assumption under the word "verified" that has not been tested, and testing it needs the checker run on a real x86 machine with the owner's copy of the game.

To reproduce the sweep: for each verified function, disassemble the original, and for each call scan forward to the next call or return for a compare on the returned register followed by a signed conditional instruction; compare the count with the signed comparisons in the rewrite.

entry.title: Finishing a large staged function: shared slots with two arities
entry.summary: A large viewer method left half-proven by an earlier attempt was carried to full verification in five stages with one rewrite. The surprises were all in the calling shapes: one slot called with two different argument counts, an entry spill that changes which object the tail compares, and a loop index that resets on exhaustion.
entry.content:
A large viewer method left half-proven by an earlier attempt was carried to full verification in five stages with one rewrite. The surprises were all in the calling shapes: one slot called with two different argument counts, an entry spill that changes which object the tail compares, and a loop index that resets on exhaustion.

What was asked

Continue the staged proof of a large function deferred as partly proven in stages: two stages already passed, two planned. Finish the remaining stages so that one rewrite passes every stage contract and the stages together reach every branch and every callee.

What was found

  • Verified One rewrite now passes four stage contracts at one thousand trials each with zero failures, bit-exact floating point, and a caught deliberately-broken version per stage. A fifth diagnostic pass proved each of eight gate-fail trials fails at exactly its gate.
  • Verified Two indirect-call slots are each invoked once with no stack arguments and once with one stack word. Stack-balance analysis shows the pushed word belongs to the following call, which takes a value-plus-flag pair; the rewrite pushes both words there with identical logged arguments and final stack pointer, confirmed by the passing runs.
  • Verified The entry code spills an object pointer over its own incoming argument slot, so the tail compares that object rather than the entry argument. The spill sits below the checker's observed stack window, and the first probe caught the misreading immediately because the original called through the wrong table.
  • Verified A count-driven search loop keeps its trip index only when it finds a match and resets it to zero when the count runs out; the probe caught the first rewrite returning the exhausted count instead.
  • Verified In contract global values, per-trial rotation needs an explicit rotation entry; a bare list of values does not rotate and silently holds its first element on every trial. The symptom was two callees that never fired because one trial type never materialised.

What was decided or recommended

The function counts as verified: every branch and every callee is reached across the stages with no narrowed comparison. The gate-diagnostic pattern (one mutant per gate, each allowed to fail only on its own trial types) is a cheap way to prove fail-edge coverage when several edges share one tail; it is worth reusing on the next staged function with shared tails.

How to reproduce it

Each stage has a machine-written contract: scripted per-call answers, fabricated heap objects with planted indirect-call targets, and pinned inputs forcing each path in turn. The checker runs original and rewrite from identical state over one thousand trials per stage and compares memory writes, stack use, outgoing calls and faults. Deliberately broken rewrites confirmed each stage catches real differences, including one caught by a single heap byte.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first stage probe faulted in the original before any new code ran, because the cascade object had been misread as the entry argument instead of the spilled object. A later probe failed only on exhaust trials, which exposed the index reset. A third showed zero failures yet was judged vacuous, which exposed the non-rotating global list. All three were contract or rewrite bugs, fixed without touching the checker.

entry.title: How many old proofs would the current checker accept
entry.summary: Asked. Proofs accepted under checker versions 1-4 predate version 3's vacuity marking and later tightenings. What share of them would the current version-6 checker still accept as they stand, and does that share differ by checker version or by kind of function?
entry.content:
Asked. Proofs accepted under checker versions 1-4 predate version 3's vacuity marking and later tightenings. What share of them would the current version-6 checker still accept as they stand, and does that share differ by checker version or by kind of function?

Method (Verified). A random sample of 180 verified functions with version 1-4 proofs was re-run through its own unchanged contracts (only the rewrite DLL path repointed) on the stock version-6 worker. FINDINGS-TBD.

What was found (Verified). RESULTS-TBD.

Two failures, both checker-side (Verified). One proof fails because both sides make more calls than the default call-log cap on a few trials; the two sides agree exactly, but the checker fails truncated trials. The other fails on a single trial where the function computes a data address that lands in executable code pages: the original reads it without remark, while the rewrite side faults because the checker revokes code pages while the rewrite runs. In both cases the rewrite mirrors the original; the check, not the rewrite, rejects the proof.

Decided. Nothing repaired (measurement lane). The two failing proofs need contract-level handling: a raised call-log cap for the first, narrowed inputs that keep computed reads out of code pages for the second. Vacuous proofs need contracts whose declared callees actually fire (details in the lane report).

Reproduce. Lane folder k-vac under the scratch area: manifest.json (sample + staged contracts), results.json (per-function class), analysis.json (shares with confidence intervals), report.md (full findings).

entry.title: Naming a batch of scanner, task, camera and cutscene functions
entry.summary: One hundred forty-nine of one hundred fifty consecutive functions were named, with the strongest new signal being that the last simple-task virtual slot is the attack method, confirmed by its only three overrides.
entry.content:
One hundred forty-nine of one hundred fifty consecutive functions were named, with the strongest new signal being that the last simple-task virtual slot is the attack method, confirmed by its only three overrides.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name and no rewriting.

What was found

  • Verified The batch splits into four clusters: entity scanners with one assess worker per ped event family, destroy-car and driveby task virtuals with their helpers, cutscene camera slot management with the animation player, and the cutscene object with draw emission, probe lighting and bounds.
  • Verified Joining several thousand vtable entries from earlier batches against the names other lanes gave confirms the task slot vocabulary: clone, task id, abort handler, per-frame processing, and first, next and control subtask methods, each agreed by dozens of prior names.
  • Verified The last simple-task virtual slot is the attack method: only three overrides exist in plain code, belonging to the fire-gun, melee-result and gang-driveby tasks, and each one calls attack routines. This sets the naming convention for that slot.
  • Verified Three tiny routines that only appear as pushed constants are animation-end callbacks, installed through one shared installer routine alongside a flag and a context pointer, each marking its own task finished.
  • Verified Six near-identical function pairs differ only in parameters such as a table word, an argument count, a track tag or a probe selector; byte-diffing each pair before naming kept them distinct.
  • Inferred Several low-confidence merged symbol labels look wrong: two encrypted stubs behave as the new and delete operators, one ubiquitous call is the event-submit helper rather than a helmet native, and the supposed task-only allocator is used by animation and cutscene constructors too.

What was decided or recommended

Forty-nine names were recorded at high confidence from slot plus shape, one hundred at medium from close reading, and one function was left empty at low confidence because its callee is unidentified. Later lanes should reuse the slot-join approach for task batches, byte-diff twin functions before naming them, and treat the low-confidence merged labels above with suspicion.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table per function with direct-call targets resolved against verified rewrites and lane names, imports, string references and constant returns; scan the code section once for callers of every batch function; read the short functions and the unclear ones fully; join vtable evidence from all earlier naming batches against lane names to derive slot meanings; byte-diff near-identical neighbours.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first evidence pass indexed the memory-mapped image by file offset instead of by address offset and decoded padding as code; decoding one known tiny function end to end exposed the mistake immediately. Two caller names used as supporting evidence appear mislabeled, so every name in this batch rests on the function's own body rather than on its callers.

entry.title: How many proofs are blind to a flipped comparison: a measurement
entry.summary: About four in ten verified proofs covering a comparison on a callee's answer cannot see that comparison's signedness being flipped, and about one in three cannot see its bound moved by one. Five spot-checks against the original found the rewrites right and only the proofs weak, but the sample is small and hand-picked.
entry.content:
About four in ten verified proofs covering a comparison on a callee's answer cannot see that comparison's signedness being flipped, and about one in three cannot see its bound moved by one. Five spot-checks against the original found the rewrites right and only the proofs weak, but the sample is small and hand-picked.

What was asked

After over a hundred verified rewrites were withdrawn because they compared a length unsigned where the original compares signed, the project needed a measurement: how many verified proofs are blind to a signedness change or an off-by-one bound on a value returned by a callee. The plan was to find such comparisons by script, build two one-change wrong versions per sampled function (other signedness, bound moved by one), run each through the function's existing contract unchanged, and count how many pass.

What was found

Verified A scripted scan found 241 verified rewrites (about three percent of the verified tree, excluding one template family handled separately) that compare a callee-returned value with an ordering comparison, directly or through one local. Sixty were sampled with a fixed seed, spread across lane kinds and sizes; 57 validated (three excluded when their correct version came back vacuous under the current driver).

Verified Of the validated functions, 20 of 45 sign-flipped wrong versions passed (44 percent, 95 percent interval 31 to 59), and 20 of 57 bound-shifted wrong versions passed (35 percent, interval 24 to 48). That implies roughly 107 sign-blind and 85 bound-blind proofs in the 241. Thirty-two of the 57 functions were blind to at least one of the two changes. Every failing wrong version failed on genuine trial differences, and the blindness was spread across lane kinds and function sizes rather than confined to one group.

Verified Five blind cases were checked against the original by reading the comparison the original actually makes. All five rewrites were right; the proofs were merely weak because the contracts never answer the callee with the values that would distinguish the mutants (a negative answer, a zero, the exact boundary).

Inferred The cause is structural, as suspected: a value a function receives directly is generated with edge cases, while a callee's answer is whatever the lane scripted, and lanes script small values that steer down the function's paths. One lane's own notes even record that its trials cover only the negative path.

What was decided or recommended

The 32 blind functions are listed in the lane's data files with the exact comparison and which wrong version passed, so re-run lanes can strengthen exactly those contracts. The recommended strengthening is to script the callee answer at the comparison boundary, one above and below it, and one large or negative value, then re-run both wrong versions and require both to fail. Extending the measurement to the full 150-function sample needs only more runs, and a random subset of the blind list still needs checking against the original.

How to reproduce it

From the repository: scan the verified rewrites for ordering comparisons whose operands resolve to callee-slot calls directly or through one local; draw the seeded stratified sample; build the sign-flip and bound-shift wrong versions with one text-level change each; assemble one proof crate holding the correct version plus both wrong versions per function; run each variant through the function's existing contract unchanged on the stock checker worker at the contract's own trial count; count passes. The lane's scratch folder holds the scripts, the sample, the per-function outcomes, and the blind list.

What was confusing or went wrong

The lane was stopped from outside midway and restarted; its scratch folder held everything, so the rerun lost no work. On resume, the first collection round reported all 60 correct runs failing, which turned out to be the collector reading the wrong verdict field rather than any real failure. Two resume-log timestamps were written from memory about fifteen minutes fast and had to be corrected from the machine clock. Two tracked verified files were found truncated or dangling, and six needed helpers from their lane's crate root, copied verbatim into the scratch crate.

entry.title: A full class batch verified, including a float returned on the x87 stack
entry.summary: A production lane verified all 42 animation-channel methods in its batch, and proved that a function returning a float on the x87 stack can be checked today with an f32 rewrite return and the x87 state comparison.
entry.content:
A production lane verified all 42 animation-channel methods in its batch, and proved that a function returning a float on the x87 stack can be checked today with an f32 rewrite return and the x87 state comparison.

What was asked

Rewrite 42 related animation-channel methods in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original, with 1,000 trials and a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All 42 methods passed 1,000 trials each with every wrong version caught; none were deferred.

Verified A Rust rewrite declared to return f32 leaves the value in the x87 ST0 register on this target, and the checker's x87 state comparison verifies it bit for bit, including signed zeros and quiet not-a-numbers. The brief lists x87 returns as not provable; that holds for doubles, but a single-precision x87 return works with no return channel compared and the x87 state check on.

Verified Indirect calls cannot be site-patched (the driver refuses anything that is not a direct call). They are intercepted by planting a stub address in the fabricated object table and having the rewrite load and call through it exactly like the original.

Verified Three separate copy and serialize loops return a reloaded count, not the last value they moved: each loop ends by loading the count into the return register after the final element. Two first attempts returned the last element and failed; reading the last register write before the return, not the loop body, gives the right answer.

What was decided or recommended

Lanes with an x87 single-precision return should attempt it with an f32 rewrite signature instead of deferring. Lanes should check what value the return register holds after a loop rather than assuming it holds the last computed value. The indirect-call planting pattern is now demonstrated and reusable.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the stock checker driver and worker; each verdict records 1,000 passing trials and each wrong-version verdict records a failure on the x87, heap, call or return comparison as appropriate.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two first attempts misread the original: a decoder slot was assumed to carry the object pointer when address arithmetic showed it carries the bit cursor, and a thread-block accessor was dereferenced once too often. A build briefly failed because a finished run still held the rewrite library file; a retry seconds later succeeded. All were fixed and re-proven in the same session.

entry.title: A stuck tick stopped the lanes: how one slow step took down three agents
entry.summary: At 18:40 on 5 October every lane the project was running stopped at once. Nothing had crashed. A chain of three ordinary things did it, and each link had looked safe on its own.
entry.content:
At 18:40 on 5 October every lane the project was running stopped at once. Nothing had crashed. A chain of three ordinary things did it, and each link had looked safe on its own.

LinkWhat happenedStatus
A finished lane left work runningA production lane ended at 17:54 and reported that nothing of its own was still running. Seventeen copies of one of its helper scripts were, and stayed busy for 52 to 117 minutes, about four processor cores between them. The watchdog stops such leftovers only when they are two and a half hours old.Verified (process list, command lines, ages)
The five-minute tick slowed to a crawlThe tick's rewrite importer reads every lane's results, about 1,500 folders, and normally takes a minute. From 18:30 it ran for more than ten, reading about 120 files a second with the disk idle and no paging. After the leftovers were stopped the same step took 57 seconds.Timing verified; the leftovers as the cause is inferred from that before and after, not proven
The supervisor waits for the tickThe supervisor starts lanes and runs the tick itself, and runs as one background task with a two-hour limit. It is written to finish by itself after 112 minutes. It was inside the tick when the 112 minutes passed, was still there when the two hours passed, and was stopped at the limit.Verified (supervisor log, task record)
Lanes are the supervisor's childrenStopping the task stopped everything it had started: three lanes that were 30 to 45 minutes into their work, among them the audit of blind proofs and the first class-completion lane.Verified

What was lost and what was not

No results were lost: lanes keep their state in their own folders and write results as they go. About two lane-hours of model work were interrupted, and for seven minutes nothing was running. A fourth lane had finished four minutes earlier and is unaffected: it verified 26 of 27 tiny forwarding functions in 25 minutes, all of them deferred as untestable by the project's earliest lanes, because the checker of that day could not follow a jump out of a function.

Changes

  • Every step of the tick has a time limit. A step that overruns is stopped with its whole process tree, the tick says so, and the remaining steps run. The limits add up to under fourteen minutes.
  • The supervisor runs no tick in the last eight minutes of its window, and the window is 100 minutes, so the worst case ends before the task's limit.
  • The lane launcher recognises a lane that was cut off from outside (its log shows a launch, work, and no exit) and resumes it from its folder instead of starting it again. The three lanes were resumed this way.
  • The watchdog stops a lane's leftover processes five minutes after that lane's launcher has logged its exit, instead of after two and a half hours.

What it says more generally

A lane's own statement that it left nothing running is a claim, not a fact; the check has to be made from outside, soon after the lane ends. And a controller that does housekeeping in its own loop inherits every way the housekeeping can stall.

Behaviour.In the workspace as crates/lf-leaderboard. Verified: 13 host tests pass; the pipeline built and tested it on Windows, Linux and macOS.
Script native handlers2,162Four short forwarding functions and a table: per native its name, its hash where known, how many script words it forwards, which of them are booleans, and how the answer is returned. Data, and useful data: it is the script machine's interface to the engine.In the workspace as crates/lf-script-natives, described as a dispatch table and not as lifted behaviour. Verified: 6 host tests pass.
Timer callback registrations81One function that makes one call through a trait, and a table of a name and an index per member. Most names are fragments of addresses, because nobody has named the things being registered. Nothing else.Not brought in and not counted as lifted. Each original passes one address to a registrar; the address is the whole content, and the lifted form replaces it with an index that means nothing yet. These are tables waiting for names.
Asset slot registrations80
Stored ratio refreshes69

Why it happened

The coordinator's brief for the second lift said to take the largest groups of same-shaped functions, in order of size. A group is large when the compiler stamped out one tiny routine hundreds of times, and the routines stamped out most often are start-up registrations and forwarders. So choosing by member count selects for the functions with the least in them. The lane did what it was asked, well, and its report said plainly where each crate's owner was unknown. The count it produced, "5,587 verified functions covered by lifted code", was true by its own definition and overstated what a port gains by at least those 230.

What a better target looks like

A class whose every method is verified: it has behaviour, it has a boundary the game itself drew, and nothing is missing in the middle. A census by class name (the part of a function's name before the last scope separator) gives, today:

MeasureValueStatus
Game functions with a class-qualified nameAbout 9,800 of 37,413Verified (census script over the inventory, the naming lanes and the verified index)
Classes with four or more named methods, all verified21 classes, 127 functions, 16,600 bytes, outside the leaderboard family: three audio voice classes, several animation channel decoders, a streaming device, a few task classesVerified
Classes with 70% or more of their bytes verified but not all467 classes, missing 1,327 functions and 60,000 bytes between themVerified
What "all verified" leaves outMethods nobody has named yet are invisible to the census. A class counted as complete may have virtual functions that are still anonymous.Known limit

Decisions

  • Lift targets are classes verified in full, not the largest shape groups. The animation channel decoders are first: 14 related classes, 100 named methods, 55 verified.
  • Production lanes take functions in address order, so a class is finished only by accident. A new kind of lane takes the missing methods of named classes, with the verified methods of the same classes named as the place to start. The first one has 42 methods of the animation channel classes.
  • A lifted function counts as lifted only if behaviour is in it. A family whose members differ only in an address is recorded as a table, and reported separately.
  • Both crates say in their own documentation that the lane's differential run against the verified rewrites has not been repeated by the pipeline. The test crates are large generated files and are still to come.

Follow-up on the 144 withdrawn rewrites

The entry "Verified, and wrong" recorded 144 rewrites of the leaderboard row collector that compared a length unsigned. A re-run lane has re-proven all 144 with the signed comparison. Its contracts script sixteen answers for the length helper, ten of them negative or edge values, and bias the other scripted answers so that those lengths reach the comparison; the unsigned mistake, run as a wrong version, fails on every one of the 144. They are back in the verified count. The same lane found the blind spot next door in the other direction: a neighbouring function of the family compares a count unsigned, its contracts script counts from 0 to 16 only, and a rewrite that compared signed would pass. That family and the 253 row-collector rewrites that were right but had the same blind proof are queued for the same treatment. Correction to the earlier entry: it gave the number of signed members as 269; by the verified index it is 253 with the family's standard name, plus a dozen named differently.

To reproduce the census: group the game's functions by the class part of their names and compare each group with the verified index.

entry.title: Float operand order needs a branch, not a black box
entry.summary: A production lane verifying audio functions found that the standard ways of pinning floating-point operand order do not work: the compiler swapped operands past both black-box barriers and opaque call boundaries, and only an explicit both-NaN branch pins the order by construction. Two functions were verified with the branch design; a third is deferred with a complete plan.
entry.content:
A production lane verifying audio functions found that the standard ways of pinning floating-point operand order do not work: the compiler swapped operands past both black-box barriers and opaque call boundaries, and only an explicit both-NaN branch pins the order by construction. Two functions were verified with the branch design; a third is deferred with a complete plan.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighbouring audio functions in Rust and prove each rewrite bit-identical to the original with the checker, including bit-exact floating-point results with matching NaN signs. Two were verified over 1200 trials each with mutants caught; the third was fully triaged and deferred for time with an executable plan.

What was found

  • Verified The compiler swaps the operands of scalar float add and multiply even when the values pass through black-box barriers and even across no-inline call boundaries. Both swaps were seen in disassembly of built rewrites. Order decides the sign of a NaN result, so a swapped build fails trials that pair two differently-signed NaNs in one operation.
  • Verified Order matters only when both operands are NaN: a single NaN forwards that NaN either way, and invalid cases yield the same default NaN either way. Both shipped rewrites therefore test the bit patterns first, forward the destination operand explicitly on both-NaN, and run a plain operation otherwise. Subtraction and comparisons need no branch.
  • Verified A build that had silently swapped an addition still passed small probes, purely because no trial paired two NaNs there. The lesson is that float contracts must include both-NaN pairs with opposing signs in the same operation, or a luck-dependent proof looks full.
  • Verified The contract lint check caught two wrong patch offsets before anything ran, exactly the failure mode it exists to stop.

What was decided or recommended

  • Both rewrites in this batch use the NaN-branch design; one was retrofitted from the opaque-call form and re-verified, because the opaque-call form is rebuild-fragile.
